findings.title: Distributed recruitment through voice, force, and partnership
findings.claim: Focus 17:64 presents satanic action as staged, distributed recruitment: voice unsettles; horse and foot contingents carry pressure outward; shared wealth and offspring embed it in ordinary life; and the promise resolves as deception. Wider contacts make this invitation and participation, not autonomous sovereignty.
findings.mechanism: The focus's audible voice and destabilizing imperative meet direct incitement in 19:83 and interwoven satanic speech in 6:112. The jlb noise-and-gathering branch meets the focus voice and the multi-direction approach in 7:17; khayl and rjl render that reach as mounted and foot force. The partnership term meets 35:40's partners and mutual promises ending in ghurur, while 4:120 explicitly limits the satanic promise to deception. 8:48 supplies an assurance-then-withdrawal pattern, and 14:22 limits satanic power to calling and the followers' response.
findings.reader_payoff: A list of tactics coheres as a sequence moving from attention to public mobilization and into property and family relations, then sustained by a false future promise.
findings.containment: This does not make every horse, loud voice, or child satanic. 8:60 presents legitimate cavalry preparedness, 16:8 horses as transport and adornment, and 31:19 measured, lowered voice. 3:14 and 57:20 permit a status overlay on horses but do not replace the literal troop reading. 14:22 bounds agency without erasing pressure. Connection targets supply Arabic text but not target morphology or lexical analysis.

epistemic.reason: A trusted cross-run finding is echoed by a legacy unbound reader walk; wider links are independently supplied as connection text, but target morphology is absent and some branch contacts remain contextual.

findings.title: Ordinary provision as a site of parasitic participation
findings.claim: The focus makes wealth and children objects of satanic partnership, while other passages present wealth and sons as provision and wealth and offspring as transient worldly adornment. A bounded analogy is that hostile participation can parasitize ordinary resources and family continuity; neither the goods nor children are inherently satanic.
findings.mechanism: The focus's partnership verb joins its wealth and offspring objects. 71:12 places wealth and sons alongside gardens and rivers as provision; 57:20 frames wealth and children as worldly adornment whose growth withers and whose life ends in ghurur; 35:40 also joins partners, mutual promises, and deception. These independent frames shift the focus from evil objects to ordinary goods and relations that can be captured by a deceptive partnership.
findings.reader_payoff: The harm appears as a hostile use of ordinary sources of livelihood and kinship, not as a condemnation of prosperity or family.
findings.containment: Circulation and parasitism are explanatory analogies, not an economic system directly specified by the verse. The HFT material has no anchor trace; connection targets provide Arabic but no morphology. The focus still states a command to share, and neither wealth nor children is intrinsically evil.

epistemic.reason: The HFT proposal and its caution are unanchored, while a trusted focus finding and independent supplied contexts ground the narrower provision-and-participation analogy.

findings.title: Exploratory rainfront overlay
findings.claim: A low-confidence, form-distant weather overlay links the focus's promise and resource imagery to expected yield that may wither: 57:20's rain genuinely grows plants, then they yellow and break, and the passage ends with worldly life as ghurur. This is not a literal weather reading of the focus's military wording.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies the jlb carrier, the khayl carrier, a promise, and ghurur; 57:20 supplies real rain, growth, withering, and the same deception term. The contact allows the branch images of a dry cloud and rain-signs to form a foil around an expected future yield, materially changing the promise into a possible but fragile harvest image.

findings.title: Visible force and false security
findings.claim: A wider contact lets the focus's cavalry be read as more than visible force: 67:20 challenges whether any army can protect and closes with ghurur, making military confidence a possible image of false security.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies a khayl carrier and a final ghurur word; 67:20 independently questions the protecting army and names delusion. Their contact shifts the payoff from the visibility of mounted force to the limits of the protection it appears to offer.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus's military image can carry a warning about trusting visible strength without denying that the horses and forces are concrete.
findings.containment: The appearance branch is an analogical, reframed root-image, not a lexical replacement for khayl. The target morphology in 67:20 is not supplied; the direct focus return is through its ghurur ending.

epistemic.reason: This uncandidate reading rests on one supplied medium-prior connection and a form-distant appearance branch; the text supports a possible image, not a firm lexical claim.
